passages.t: Twenty years, and a people turning back
passages.happening:
The men of Kiriath-jearim take the ark into the house of Abinadab on the hill, and set apart his son Eleazar to guard it (verse 1). “And from that day a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim. And all the house of Israel mourned and sought after the LORD” (verse 2).

Samuel speaks to all Israel. “If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then rid yourselves of the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines” (verse 3). ‘So the Israelites put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and served only the LORD’ (verse 4).

Samuel gathers all Israel to Mizpah to pray for them (verse 5). There they draw water and pour it out before the LORD. They fast, and they confess, “We have sinned against the LORD” (verse 6). And Samuel judges Israel at Mizpah.
passages.hearers:
Samuel has been out of sight since chapter 3, while the ark's story played out. He returns now as a grown leader.

The twenty years mark the time until Israel's turning, not the ark's whole stay. It stayed at Kiriath-jearim, apart from Israel's worship, until David brought it to Jerusalem, a good deal longer.

The Baals and Ashtoreths were the chief god and goddess of Canaan's religion. Baal was a storm god believed to bring the rain and the crops, and Ashtoreth, known elsewhere as Astarte, was a goddess of fertility and war. For farmers who lived by the rain, worshiping them beside the LORD seemed only sensible. That is why Israel kept falling into it. Samuel asks for the LORD only.

In this chapter repentance is not a feeling. It is a turning, with things done: the rival gods put away, a gathering, a fast, a plain confession.

Pouring out water before the LORD is found nowhere else in the Old Testament as part of an assembly of repentance. What it meant is not certain. Some see a sign of humility, like pouring out the heart. Others think it pictured the people's helplessness, or a break with the past. The verb is the one used when Hannah poured out her soul before the LORD (1:15). The mother's private prayer and the nation's public repentance are joined by one word.

Mizpah, whose name means watchtower, was a town in Benjamin, usually placed at Tell en-Nasbeh, a few miles north of Jerusalem. The tribes had gathered there before.
passages.later:
Joshua had called for the same turning at Shechem: “get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel” (Joshua 24:23), as Jacob once had told his household (Genesis 35:2).

Lamentations uses the picture of pouring out: “Pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord” (Lamentations 2:19).
passages.asks: Samuel told Israel that returning to the LORD meant putting other gods away. Ask what you keep beside God, just in case, the way Israel's farmers kept the Baals. And ask what turning back would look like in things done, not only in feelings.

passages.t: The LORD thunders, and a stone called Ebenezer
passages.happening:
The Philistines hear that Israel has gathered at Mizpah, and their rulers march up. Israel is afraid, and the people beg Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines” (verse 8).

Samuel offers a young lamb as a whole burnt offering, and he cries out to the LORD for Israel, ‘and the LORD answered him’ (verse 9). “As the Philistines drew near to fight against Israel, Samuel was sacrificing the burnt offering. But that day the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel” (verse 10). Israel chases them as far as Beth-car (verse 11).

Samuel sets up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and names it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us” (verse 12).

The Philistines are subdued and stop invading Israel's land, and ‘the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel’ (verse 13). The towns from Ekron to Gath that the Philistines had taken are given back, and there is peace with the Amorites (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This chapter answers chapter 4 point by point. There Israel lost at a place called Ebenezer. Here a stone named Ebenezer marks a victory. There the ark was carried out as a weapon. Here the ark is nowhere in view, and the people seek the LORD himself.

It also looks like a story from Judges: the people turn from other gods, they cry out, and God saves them. But there is no warrior hero. Samuel's weapons are prayer and sacrifice, and the battle is won by the LORD's thunder while Samuel is still at the altar. Hannah's song had said, ‘He will thunder from heaven against them’ (2:10).

The whole burnt offering was burned entirely on the altar, a sign of complete devotion. Setting up a stone to mark a place where God had acted was an old custom in Israel.

Ebenezer means stone of help. Thus far can mean as far as this place, or until now, and both may be meant. The two places called Ebenezer seem to be different, so the naming may be deliberate: the name of Israel's disgrace becomes a memorial of God's help.

The Amorites here means the older peoples of the hill country of Canaan.
passages.later:
Samuel is remembered as one of Israel's great intercessors. Through Jeremiah, God names him beside Moses: “Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before Me, My heart would not go out to this people” (Jeremiah 15:1).

The word help returns in the psalms: “My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (Psalm 121:2). And memorial stones go back to Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:18) and to the stones from the Jordan in Joshua's day (Joshua 4:7).
passages.hard:
If the Philistines were subdued all the days of Samuel, why are they still pressing on Israel a few chapters later?

Verse 13 says the Philistines stopped invading Israel's land and that the LORD's hand was against them all Samuel's days. Yet in chapters 9, 10 and 13 there are Philistine posts in Israel's land, and the Philistines control the making of iron weapons. Readers handle this in several ways. Some take verse 13 to mean that the Philistines made no further great invasion while Samuel judged, while local garrisons and pressure went on. Others note that Samuel's active leadership gave way to Saul's, and that the renewed Philistine threat belongs to Saul's reign, when Samuel was old. Many critical scholars think the chapter comes from a source that idealized Samuel's time, set beside other sources with a different picture.

Readers across these views agree on the chapter's purpose. It shows what deliverance looks like when Israel turns back and relies on the LORD, in contrast to the king who will be demanded in the next chapter.
passages.asks: Samuel set up a stone and said, ‘Thus far the LORD has helped us.’ Ask where you would set up such a stone in your own life. And ask whether you have asked anyone to keep crying out to God for you, as Israel asked Samuel.

passages.happening:
“So Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. Every year he would go on a circuit from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places” (verses 15-16).

“Then he would return to Ramah because his home was there, and there he judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
These verses sum up Samuel's career in the style of the book of Judges, as if closing an era. He is the last of the judges, and in some ways the greatest: a prophet, a priest who offers sacrifice, and a deliverer.

The word judge means more than deciding cases in court. It means to rule, to lead, and to set things right. The judges of the book of Judges were deliverers and leaders, and Samuel is both.

His yearly circuit took him to Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah and back home to Ramah, a fairly small region in the central hill country. That suggests his direct work as judge was centered there, not across the whole land.

The chapter has shown a better way than the one Israel will now ask for. That makes the next chapter all the more painful.
passages.later:
Paul, preaching in Acts, tells this part of Israel's story in one line: ‘After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet’ (Acts 13:20).

Hebrews names Samuel among those ‘who through faith conquered kingdoms, administered justice, and gained what was promised’ (Hebrews 11:32-33).
passages.asks: Samuel served in the same few towns, year after year, for the rest of his life. Ask what faithfulness in a small circle looks like for you. And ask whether you value the people who serve that way, without fame or a king's crown.
